variants.title: Run the search as an experiment
variants.context: NAS is a controlled experiment loop: declare the deployment envelope, define a legal search space, propose candidates, measure them under one versioned proxy protocol, update the Pareto frontier, then retrain finalists independently.
variants.prompt: A team starts a NAS project for an on-device vision model. Put the loop stages in order.

items.text: Measure a comparable proxy: train or inherit weights under one versioned protocol and record quality, cost, and failures.
Retrain finalists independently: fresh initialization, repeated seeds, full budget, and untouched test evidence.
Define a legal search space: operations, connections, depth, width, and shape constraints that can be built and measured.
Update the Pareto frontier: retain candidates not dominated across quality, latency, memory, energy, and uncertainty.
Propose the next candidates: allocate evaluation budget with evolution, Bayesian optimization, or a differentiable relaxation.
Declare the deployment envelope: quality floor, p95 latency, memory, energy, hardware, and prohibited operations.

variants.hint: The constraint that decides what counts as legal comes before anything is proposed.
variants.explanation: The envelope and the space define what a candidate may even be, so scoring and selection only mean something inside them.

variants.title: Run the search as an experiment
variants.context: NAS is a controlled experiment loop: declare the deployment envelope, define a legal search space, propose candidates, measure them under one versioned proxy protocol, update the Pareto frontier, then retrain finalists independently.
variants.prompt: Half the proposed candidates fail to build because their residual shapes do not match. Put the stages in order for the corrected run.

items.text: Define a legal search space where conditional constraints reject invalid residual shapes before submission.
Propose candidates whose mutations either preserve validity or repair the graph deterministically.
Measure a comparable proxy on the candidates that now decode into trainable, exportable models.
Update the Pareto frontier from evidence that no longer mixes built and unbuildable candidates.
Declare the deployment envelope again, including the operators the target runtime actually executes.

variants.hint: Which stage owns the rule that every encoded candidate must decode into a valid model?
variants.explanation: Feasibility belongs in the search space, because a space that emits unbuildable candidates spends budget producing no evidence.

variants.title: Run the search as an experiment
variants.context: NAS is a controlled experiment loop: declare the deployment envelope, define a legal search space, propose candidates, measure them under one versioned proxy protocol, update the Pareto frontier, then retrain finalists independently.
variants.prompt: The search finished and a supernet-inherited winner is being proposed for release. Put the remaining stages in order.

items.text: Update the Pareto frontier so the shortlist keeps non-dominated candidates rather than one blended winner.
Validate the retrained finalists on target hardware and on test evidence the search never touched.
Measure the comparable proxy scores that ranked the candidates during search.
Retrain finalists from random initialization with full data, full budget, and repeated seeds.

variants.hint: What is the proxy allowed to decide, and what must it never decide alone?
variants.explanation: A proxy shortlists; it does not certify. The released architecture is measured independently of the signal that guided the search.

variants.title: Audit the proxy before scaling
variants.context: A cheap proxy is useful only when it preserves the rankings full training would produce. Audit it on sampled candidates against a matched full-training protocol before you scale the search, and never publish inherited weights as final evidence.
variants.prompt: A team wants to cut candidate cost by training each one for a tenth of the usual schedule. Put the fidelity audit in order.

items.text: Score them with the short proxy and with a matched full-training protocol across repeated seeds.
Sample candidates across architecture families, sizes, and predicted quality bands.
Measure rank agreement, systematic bias, error spread, and family-specific reversals.
Repeat hardware profiling on the actual compiler, precision, batch shape, and target device.
Use the proxy to shortlist, then retrain the finalists from scratch for the final evidence.

variants.hint: You cannot judge a proxy against itself.
variants.explanation: Proxy fidelity is measured against a matched full-training protocol on a spread of families, since reversals are usually family specific.

variants.title: Audit the proxy before scaling
variants.context: A cheap proxy is useful only when it preserves the rankings full training would produce. Audit it on sampled candidates against a matched full-training protocol before you scale the search, and never publish inherited weights as final evidence.
variants.prompt: A low-resolution proxy is suspected of favoring one architecture family. Put the audit steps in order for that suspicion.

items.text: Shortlist with the proxy only after the per-family agreement is known, then retrain from scratch.
Sample candidates from the suspected family and from the families it is beating.
Measure pairwise agreement separately per family so a family-specific reversal cannot average away.
Score every sampled candidate with the proxy and with full training under matched seeds.
Repeat the hardware profile at the real input shape rather than the reduced proxy resolution.

variants.hint: An aggregate correlation can hide a reversal that only affects one family.
variants.explanation: Rank agreement must be sliced by family, because a proxy that is right on average can still invert the comparison that decides the winner.

variants.title: Audit the proxy before scaling
variants.context: A cheap proxy is useful only when it preserves the rankings full training would produce. Audit it on sampled candidates against a matched full-training protocol before you scale the search, and never publish inherited weights as final evidence.
variants.prompt: Weight inheritance from a supernet is the proposed proxy. Put the audit steps in order.

items.text: Profile the discretized candidates on the target compiler and precision, not on the supernet graph.
Measure how far weight-sharing bias moves the ranking against independent training.
Score each one with inherited weights and with an independently trained matched protocol.
Sample candidates spanning the supernet's operation choices and size bands.
Shortlist with the supernet, then retrain finalists from fresh initialization before any claim.

variants.hint: Discretization and weight sharing each need confirmation of their own.
variants.explanation: Differentiable search needs independent confirmation, so inherited supernet weights shortlist candidates and never serve as final evidence.

variants.title: Account for the search budget
variants.context: Accelerator-hours measure total work; wall time divides that work across parallel accelerators. Parallelism lowers elapsed time but never lowers accelerator-hours, and failed jobs and finalist retraining still count against the budget.
variants.prompt: A search trains 600 candidates at 5 accelerator-hours each. Another 60 jobs crash after averaging 2 accelerator-hours apiece. How many accelerator-hours does the search consume?
variants.hint: Every job that touched an accelerator spent budget, whether or not it produced a score.
variants.explanation: Failed jobs and retries are part of the search cost, so budget accounting sums all consumed work rather than only successful evaluations.

mistakes.feedback: That counts only the successful candidates and drops the 120 hours the crashed jobs consumed.
That charges each crashed job the full 5 hours instead of the 2 it actually used.

variants.title: Account for the search budget
variants.context: Accelerator-hours measure total work; wall time divides that work across parallel accelerators. Parallelism lowers elapsed time but never lowers accelerator-hours, and failed jobs and finalist retraining still count against the budget.
variants.prompt: A search has 9,600 accelerator-hours of work and runs on 64 accelerators at full utilization. Ignoring queueing overhead, what is the wall time in hours?
variants.hint: Parallel resources split the same total work.
variants.explanation: Wall time is total accelerator-hours divided by the number of parallel accelerators, while the accelerator-hours and the bill stay unchanged.

mistakes.feedback: That reports total work as elapsed time and ignores the 64 accelerators running in parallel.
That multiplies by the accelerator count; parallel accelerators divide elapsed time, they do not add work.

variants.title: Account for the search budget
variants.context: Accelerator-hours measure total work; wall time divides that work across parallel accelerators. Parallelism lowers elapsed time but never lowers accelerator-hours, and failed jobs and finalist retraining still count against the budget.
variants.prompt: Proxy search spent 1,200 accelerator-hours. Three finalists must then be retrained from scratch on 4 seeds each, at 90 accelerator-hours per run. What is the total accelerator-hours for the project?
variants.hint: Confirmation is a budget line, not a rounding error.
variants.explanation: Finalist retraining across repeated seeds is part of the search budget, because a result that was never confirmed independently cannot ship.

mistakes.feedback: That is only the retraining work and leaves out the 1,200 hours the proxy search already spent.
That retrains each finalist once instead of on all 4 seeds.

variants.title: Turn evidence into a decision
variants.context: Candidate evidence becomes a decision in stages: record measured objectives with their protocol identity, apply hard feasibility gates, keep the non-dominated candidates, then retrain and profile a small finalist set.
variants.prompt: A generation returns 200 measured candidates. Put the decision stages in order.

items.text: Keep the candidates that are not dominated across the product's independent objectives.
Apply the feasibility gate to reject sub-floor quality, p95 latency over budget, and memory overflow.
Retrain, repeat seeds, profile on target hardware, and compare the finalists with a strong manual baseline.
Record each candidate's quality, latency distribution, memory, energy, failures, and protocol identity.

variants.hint: A hard constraint is not something a good score can buy back.
variants.explanation: Hard deployment constraints filter candidates before any trade-off is compared, so the frontier only ever contains shippable options.

variants.title: Turn evidence into a decision
variants.context: Candidate evidence becomes a decision in stages: record measured objectives with their protocol identity, apply hard feasibility gates, keep the non-dominated candidates, then retrain and profile a small finalist set.
variants.prompt: The top candidate on a blended reward score needs an operator the target runtime cannot execute. Put the stages in order, showing where it drops out.

items.text: Rebuild the frontier from the feasible candidates only.
Record its measured objectives together with the operator set the graph requires.
Review the surviving finalists on target hardware against the manual baseline.
Reject it at the feasibility gate, since an unsupported operator is a contract violation.

variants.hint: Ask which stage a weighted reward score would have let this candidate skip.
variants.explanation: One blended score hides which constraint was violated, so feasibility stays a separate hard gate ahead of the trade-off comparison.

variants.title: Turn evidence into a decision
variants.context: Candidate evidence becomes a decision in stages: record measured objectives with their protocol identity, apply hard feasibility gates, keep the non-dominated candidates, then retrain and profile a small finalist set.
variants.prompt: Two feasible candidates have overlapping quality intervals but different latency tails. Put the stages in order.

items.text: Confirm both clear the hard gates for quality floor, memory, and p95 latency.
Retrain both from fresh initialization and compare p95 and p99 on target hardware before choosing.
Record mean and spread across training seeds, data order, and hardware runs for both.
Keep both on the frontier, since neither dominates once the intervals overlap.

variants.hint: Domination is a claim about intervals, not about point estimates.
variants.explanation: Objectives are reported with uncertainty, so two candidates whose intervals overlap both stay on the frontier until confirmation separates them.

variants.title: Keep the final claim honest
variants.context: Repeatedly selecting on validation scores turns that split into training signal for the controller. Keep search training, controller validation, selection validation, and final test evidence distinct, and compare against a no-search baseline.
variants.prompt: A team compared 3,000 candidates on one validation set and now reports that same validation score as the headline result. What is the core problem?
options: Repeated selection turned that split into controller training signal, so the score is optimistic.
The candidates should have been ranked on a rolling average rather than one final checkpoint.
The validation set was too small to separate 3,000 candidates with statistical confidence.
optionFeedback: Correct: every selection round fits the controller to that split, so the winner's score is inflated by the winner's curse.
Checkpoint choice adds noise, and it is not what makes a repeatedly selected score optimistic.
Set size matters, but the flaw here would survive even a very large validation set.
variants.hint: Count how many times a decision was made using that split.
variants.explanation: Selection on a split is optimization against it, so the final claim needs test evidence frozen until the candidates and decision rules are fixed.

variants.title: Keep the final claim honest
variants.context: Repeatedly selecting on validation scores turns that split into training signal for the controller. Keep search training, controller validation, selection validation, and final test evidence distinct, and compare against a no-search baseline.
variants.prompt: A NAS result beats the manual production architecture by 0.4 quality points, but that baseline was trained with a quarter of the final budget. What must happen before the claim ships?
options: Publish the gap alongside the number of candidates the controller evaluated during search.
Repeat the whole search with more seeds so the 0.4 point gap gains a confidence interval.
Retrain the manual baseline with the same final data, budget, and tuning, then compare again.
optionFeedback: Reporting candidate counts is good practice, but it does not repair an unequal comparison.
More seeds tighten the interval around a gap that is still measured against an under-trained baseline.
Correct: comparisons only mean something at equal training and tuning budgets, otherwise the search is being credited with extra compute.
variants.hint: What is actually different between the two models being compared?
variants.explanation: A discovered architecture must beat a strong manual baseline and simpler scaled baselines under equal training and tuning budgets.

variants.title: Keep the final claim honest
variants.context: Repeatedly selecting on validation scores turns that split into training signal for the controller. Keep search training, controller validation, selection validation, and final test evidence distinct, and compare against a no-search baseline.
variants.prompt: Inherited supernet weights already show one family winning, and shipping those weights would save a week of retraining. What should the team do?
options: Shortlist with the supernet, then retrain the finalists from fresh initialization for final evidence.
Publish the inherited weights, since the supernet trained every candidate under one shared protocol.
Extend supernet training until the inherited ranking stops changing across repeated seeds.
optionFeedback: Correct: the proxy chooses who is measured, and the released model is confirmed by independent retraining.
Shared training is exactly the problem: weight sharing biases the comparison it is being used to settle.
A stable inherited ranking is still an inherited ranking, and stability is not independence.
variants.hint: Which evidence is independent of the signal that chose the winner?
variants.explanation: Inherited weights are search evidence, not release evidence, so finalists are retrained from scratch and measured on untouched data.
